metadata.name: cat
metadata.description: Display file contents or concatenate multiple files

installation.note: cat is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: cat (concatenate) displays the contents of files on the standard output. It can read single or multiple files and concatenate them together. Despite its name, it's most commonly used to quickly view file contents rather than concatenate.
when_to_use: Pipe file contents to other commands
Check file content without opening an editor

syntax.description: Display contents of FILE(s). Multiple files are concatenated in order. If no file is specified or FILE is -, cat reads from standard input.

misconceptions.title: cat is only for concatenation
misconceptions.misconception: cat is primarily used to concatenate files
misconceptions.reality: While cat can concatenate files, it's most commonly used to display file contents. The name comes from 'concatenate' but viewing is the primary use case.
misconceptions.tip: cat is mainly for viewing files quickly. Use it for small files, not large ones (use less or more instead).

misconceptions.title: cat is good for large files
misconceptions.misconception: cat works well for any file size
misconceptions.reality: cat outputs the entire file at once, which can flood your terminal. Use less or more for large files to view them page by page.
misconceptions.tip: For large files, use less (allows scrolling) or more (page-by-page). cat is best for small files only.

common_pitfalls.description: cat displays entire file content at once, flooding terminal
common_pitfalls.solution: Use less file.txt for large files (allows scrolling with arrow keys, press 'q' to quit). Or use more for page-by-page viewing.

common_pitfalls.description: Displaying binary files can corrupt terminal display
common_pitfalls.solution: Never use cat on binary files. Use file command to check file type first, or use hexdump/xxd to view binary content safely.

common_pitfalls.description: When creating files with cat > file, forgetting to press Ctrl+D
common_pitfalls.solution: Press Ctrl+D (not Ctrl+C which cancels) to finish input and save the file. Ctrl+C discards the file.

best_practices: Use cat for small text files only
Use -n for line numbers when referencing specific lines
Use -A to see all special characters and formatting
Combine with grep: cat file.txt | grep pattern
Use cat with redirection to create files: cat > file.txt
Avoid cat with binary files - can corrupt terminal display
For large files, use less or more instead
performance_tips: cat is very fast for small files
For large files, less is more efficient (loads as needed)
Avoid piping large cat output unnecessarily - use direct file access when possible

additional_notes.primary_use: Despite the name 'concatenate', cat is most commonly used to view file contents
additional_notes.small_files: Best for files that fit on one screen - use less/more for larger files
additional_notes.redirection: Common pattern: cat file1 file2 > combined.txt to concatenate and save
additional_notes.heredoc: cat can be used with heredoc syntax: cat << EOF > file.txt
additional_notes.binary_warning: Never use cat on binary files - can corrupt terminal display with control characters
